questions.skillExplanation: Q14 tests whether the learner recognizes that extensive planning creates an expectation of speaking, while the actual result is inability to say anything; the clauses therefore stand in contrast.
reasoningOperations: Identify the expectation created by planning.
Compare that expectation with the opposite outcome.
Select an adversative coordinator.
questions.questionMechanism: The blank joins two independent clauses whose propositions conflict, so discourse relation determines the coordinator.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: All four options are common connectors, but only 'but' preserves the expectation-versus-result contrast.
questions.correctRationale: Planning for several days should make speaking more likely, yet she could not say a word; 'but' explicitly marks that contrast, so A is correct.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: 'spent several days planning' contrasts with 'couldn’t say a word'

B.rationale: 'if' introduces a condition, but the second clause is an actual event, not a condition.
B.misconceptionTarget: Treating any clause linker as interchangeable.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Both events are asserted as facts.

C.rationale: 'or' presents alternatives, while the sentence describes two events that both happened.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The clauses are not alternatives.

D.rationale: 'so' would say the planning caused her silence, which is opposite to the intended surprising contrast.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Planning creates an expectation that she would speak.

studentFailureModes: Choosing by punctuation instead of clause meaning.
Treating 'so' as a generic connector for any second result.
misconceptionsTargeted: Coordinating conjunctions can be selected without identifying the logical relation.
Earlier action automatically causes the later event.

shallowRecall.explanation: The conjunction is selected from the discourse relation between two propositions.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Build conjunction items around a strong expectation that the second clause clearly confirms or violates.
depthAdjustmentStrategies: Make the expected outcome implicit and require readers to infer why the second clause is surprising.

evidenceReferences.quoteOrDescription: 'spent several days planning' contrasts with 'couldn’t say a word'

questions.skillExplanation: Q15 requires locating movie-watching in an unfinished time window extending to now: the speaker cannot give an opinion because the movie has not been watched yet.
reasoningOperations: Use the future plan to infer the viewing has not happened.
Choose present perfect for a past-to-present experience state.
questions.questionMechanism: The future sentence 'I'll probably watch it this Saturday' establishes non-occurrence up to the present, licensing negative present perfect.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: The distractors are grammatical-looking tense forms, but only present perfect naturally expresses 'not yet experienced by now.'
questions.correctRationale: The speaker currently lacks an opinion and plans to watch later, so 'haven’t seen' correctly means the experience has not occurred up to now; C is correct.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The speaker cannot judge the movie now and will probably watch it this Saturday.

A.rationale: 'am not seeing' describes a current progressive situation, not a missing life/recent experience.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The issue is whether the event has occurred before now.

B.rationale: 'don’t see' suggests a habitual or general state, not 'have not watched yet.'
B.misconceptionTarget: Using simple present for an unfinished experience window.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: A specific future viewing is planned.

D.rationale: 'won’t see' says the speaker will not watch it, contradicting the next sentence.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The next sentence says the speaker probably will watch it.

studentFailureModes: Ignoring the future sentence.
Mapping 'now' automatically to present tense.
misconceptionsTargeted: Present perfect can be replaced by simple present whenever the consequence is current.
Future context does not constrain the earlier blank.

shallowRecall.explanation: The tense is determined by a temporal relation spanning present state and future plan.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Use a present consequence plus a future plan to force interpretation of an uncompleted experience up to now.
simplificationConstraints: Keep a clear future plan to watch the movie.
depthAdjustmentStrategies: Remove 'because' and make the missing experience inferable from a subtler conversational response.

evidenceReferences.quoteOrDescription: The speaker cannot judge the movie now and will probably watch it this Saturday.

questions.skillExplanation: Q16 asks the learner to map a flat, emotionless speaking style onto the stereotypical property of a robot.
reasoningOperations: Extract the voice properties: no pitch variation and no emotional cue.
Map those properties to the best comparison noun.
questions.questionMechanism: The second sentence defines the relevant features, and the first asks for a comparison entity that bundles those features.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: 'Father,' 'foreigner,' and 'radio' can all answer 'like a ___' grammatically, but they do not entail mechanical, emotionless delivery.
questions.correctRationale: No ups and downs in the voice and no detectable emotion describe robotic speech, so D is correct.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: 'no ups and downs in his voice' and inability to tell whether he is happy or sad

A.rationale: Being a father does not imply flat or emotionless speech.
A.misconceptionTarget: Using arbitrary person categories as personality cues.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The stem gives vocal, not family-role, evidence.

B.rationale: Being foreign does not imply monotone or emotionlessness.
B.misconceptionTarget: Relying on stereotypes rather than stated acoustic features.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The clues concern prosody, not nationality.

C.rationale: A radio can produce voices but does not itself imply flat emotional delivery.
C.misconceptionTarget: Choosing an object associated with sound instead of matching the described manner.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Radios can broadcast highly expressive voices.

studentFailureModes: Selecting any noun related to speaking or sound.
Missing that the second sentence functions as a definition.
misconceptionsTargeted: Similes can be solved by topic association alone.
A radio necessarily sounds monotone.

shallowRecall.explanation: The learner interprets descriptive features and maps them to a figurative comparison.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Define a comparison indirectly through two observable traits rather than naming the trait itself.
simplificationConstraints: Keep both flat-pitch and emotionless clues.
depthAdjustmentStrategies: Use less explicit prosody clues, such as identical delivery of good and bad news.

evidenceReferences.quoteOrDescription: 'no ups and downs in his voice' and inability to tell whether he is happy or sad

questions.skillExplanation: Q17 tests the verb 'miss' meaning to feel the absence of something familiar, not fail to hit or fail to notice.
reasoningOperations: Use the move from city to country as a change of environment.
Infer that the formerly familiar city noise becomes absent and unexpectedly desired.
questions.questionMechanism: The context creates a before-after contrast in environment, so the target verb must express reaction to an absent former feature.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: The surprising object 'the noise in the city' makes 'miss' less formulaic and tests contextual sense selection.
questions.correctRationale: Once Jasmine is in the country, city noise is absent; starting to miss it means she feels its absence despite having chosen the country, so C is correct.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: She moved to the country and then reacted to 'the noise in the city.'

A.rationale: 'enjoy' would normally describe experiencing the noise, but she is now away from the city.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The city noise is no longer present.

B.rationale: 'mind' means be bothered by; the sentence's surprise is that she longs for something she expected to leave behind.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: She is in the country after deliberately leaving the city.

D.rationale: 'notice' requires perceiving the noise, yet she has just left the place where it occurs.
D.misconceptionTarget: Ignoring physical availability of the object.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The relevant noise is in the city.

studentFailureModes: Using only the most familiar dictionary sense of 'miss'.
Ignoring that the location change controls which actions are possible.
misconceptionsTargeted: Polysemous verbs have one fixed translation.
A person must currently perceive something in order to miss it.

shallowRecall.explanation: The item requires sense disambiguation from a change-of-location context.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Test polysemy by placing a familiar verb in a context that blocks its most literal sense.
depthAdjustmentStrategies: Make the former city feature implicit and require readers to recover it from an earlier sentence.

evidenceReferences.quoteOrDescription: She moved to the country and then reacted to 'the noise in the city.'

questions.skillExplanation: Q18 requires judging excuse quality from the boss's knowledge that the employee can walk to work in five minutes; traffic therefore cannot plausibly explain lateness.
reasoningOperations: Infer that traffic is irrelevant to a five-minute walk.
Evaluate the excuse negatively.
Select the superlative adjective expressing the strongest negative judgment.
questions.questionMechanism: The item embeds pragmatic contradiction: the offered cause cannot affect the actual commute method.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: Several superlatives are grammatically possible, but only 'worst' encodes the excuse's lack of credibility.
questions.correctRationale: If work is only a five-minute walk away, traffic is an especially implausible reason for lateness, making it the 'worst' excuse; D is correct.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The boss knows it only takes five minutes to walk to work.

A.rationale: An excuse may be easy to say, but the sentence evaluates plausibility, not production effort.
A.misconceptionTarget: Choosing an adjective that can modify 'excuse' without tracking the intended judgment.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The walking fact makes the excuse unbelievable.

B.rationale: Nothing establishes the historical age of the excuse.
B.misconceptionTarget: Importing a common phrase instead of using contextual evidence.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: No time-history comparison is given.

C.rationale: Calling it smartest conflicts with the boss's knowledge that exposes the excuse immediately.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The boss knows traffic should not matter.

studentFailureModes: Choosing based on common collocation such as 'oldest excuse'.
Failing to connect walking with traffic irrelevance.
misconceptionsTargeted: Any conventional-sounding phrase can override context.
Traffic can delay all commutes regardless of mode.

shallowRecall.explanation: The learner must evaluate causal plausibility from world knowledge explicitly activated by the stem.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Create evaluative vocabulary items where one concrete fact invalidates an otherwise common excuse.
depthAdjustmentStrategies: Replace the direct walking statement with two clues that indirectly reveal traffic is irrelevant.

evidenceReferences.quoteOrDescription: The boss knows it only takes five minutes to walk to work.

questions.skillExplanation: Q19 jointly tests that 'housework' is an uncountable singular subject and that the work receives the action of sharing, requiring singular passive 'is shared.'
reasoningOperations: Identify 'housework' as the grammatical subject.
Determine that family members distribute the housework rather than housework distributing something.
Apply singular agreement in passive voice.
questions.questionMechanism: Each option manipulates voice and/or agreement, so the learner must satisfy both semantic role and number.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: The follow-up 'Everyone’s got their own job to do' confirms distribution of tasks, strengthening the passive interpretation.
questions.correctRationale: Housework is distributed among the parents and children, so passive voice is needed; 'housework' takes singular agreement, yielding 'is shared,' A.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: 'between them and their kids' plus 'Everyone’s got their own job to do' shows distribution of housework.

B.rationale: 'are shared' has the right passive meaning but wrongly treats uncountable 'housework' as plural.
B.misconceptionTarget: Assuming -work refers to many chores and therefore takes plural agreement.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The head noun 'housework' is grammatically singular/uncountable.

C.rationale: 'shares' makes housework the agent doing the sharing.
C.misconceptionTarget: Ignoring semantic roles when active morphology is grammatical.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: People share the housework; the housework is the thing distributed.

D.rationale: 'share' is active and also lacks agreement with the singular subject.
D.misconceptionTarget: Selecting a familiar verb form without checking subject and voice.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The subject is singular and receives the action.

studentFailureModes: Treating meaning and agreement as separate and checking only one.
Interpreting an uncountable mass noun as plural because it contains many tasks.
misconceptionsTargeted: Passive voice is optional when the same verb is present.
Semantic plurality determines grammatical agreement for mass nouns.

shallowRecall.explanation: Correct selection requires simultaneous role assignment and agreement.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Make grammar distractors cross two dimensions so partial knowledge is insufficient.
simplificationConstraints: Keep 'housework' as subject and an explicit distribution clue.
depthAdjustmentStrategies: Remove the second sentence and rely on the prepositional phrase to establish passive roles.

evidenceReferences.quoteOrDescription: 'between them and their kids' plus 'Everyone’s got their own job to do' shows distribution of housework.

questions.skillExplanation: Q20 tests possessive pronoun substitution: after contrasting 'another dentist' with the previous dentist, 'mine' stands for 'my dentist.'
reasoningOperations: Establish that the person who pulled the tooth was the speaker's previous dentist.
Recognize that a subject noun phrase is required before 'pulled out'.
Use possessive pronoun 'mine' to replace 'my dentist' without repeating the noun.
questions.questionMechanism: The blank is both the subject of the clause and a contrastive possessive reference to the speaker's dentist.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: The surface forms I/me/myself are highly familiar, but only 'mine' can stand independently as a possessive noun phrase meaning 'my dentist.'
questions.correctRationale: The sentence contrasts another dentist with the speaker's current/previous one; 'mine' independently means 'my dentist' and can serve as the subject, so C is correct.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: 'another dentist' supplies the recoverable noun for possessive 'mine.'

A.rationale: 'I pulled out a good tooth' would make the speaker, not the dentist, perform the extraction.
A.misconceptionTarget: Ignoring semantic role and antecedent contrast.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The complaint is about a dentist's mistake.

B.rationale: Object-case 'me' cannot function as the subject of 'pulled out.'
B.misconceptionTarget: Using pronoun meaning without checking syntactic case.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The blank directly precedes the finite verb as subject.

D.rationale: 'myself' requires a licensed reflexive/emphatic relation to 'I' and would again make the speaker the actor.
D.misconceptionTarget: Treating all first-person pronouns as interchangeable.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The intended actor is the speaker's dentist.

studentFailureModes: Reading 'mine' only as ownership of objects, not people/roles recoverable from context.
Selecting 'I' because it is the usual subject form without checking who did the dentistry.
misconceptionsTargeted: Possessive pronouns cannot replace human-role noun phrases.
Subject case alone guarantees semantic correctness.

shallowRecall.explanation: The learner resolves a contrastive antecedent and nominal ellipsis.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Test possessive pronouns with an explicit contrast noun ('another X') that licenses an elliptical 'mine/yours/his.'
depthAdjustmentStrategies: Move the antecedent to a previous sentence so the learner must resolve it across discourse.

evidenceReferences.quoteOrDescription: 'another dentist' supplies the recoverable noun for possessive 'mine.'

questions.skillExplanation: Q21 asks the learner to distinguish a completed past portion of an unfinished report from ongoing or future actions.
reasoningOperations: Use 'this afternoon' as a completed past reference period in the conversation.
Interpret 'most of it' as a completed portion.
Contrast that completion with the future plan to finish the remainder by Friday.
questions.questionMechanism: The report as a whole is unfinished, but a large subpart was completed earlier; tense choice must track the subevent rather than the whole task.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: The dialogue tempts learners to overfocus on the unfinished report and choose a future or progressive form.
questions.correctRationale: Linda states that most of the report was completed this afternoon and only the remainder is future work; simple past 'I did' fits, so B is correct.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: 'this afternoon' marks the completed work; 'I’ll finish it by Friday' reserves only the remainder for the future.

A.rationale: 'would do' needs a conditional, reported-future, or habitual frame absent here.
A.misconceptionTarget: Choosing a modal because the report remains unfinished.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The clause reports an actual completed action.

C.rationale: 'was doing' presents an action in progress and does not naturally assert completion of 'most of it.'

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: 'most of it' is offered as progress already achieved.

D.rationale: 'I’ll do most of it this afternoon' conflicts because the afternoon work is reported as already done in this exchange.
D.misconceptionTarget: Ignoring the temporal adverb's discourse reference.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The future action is separately expressed as finishing by Friday.

studentFailureModes: Treating an unfinished whole as forcing future tense for every part.
Choosing progressive merely because the work took time.
misconceptionsTargeted: Tense must describe the whole project rather than the referenced subevent.
Past progressive entails completion of a quantified amount.

shallowRecall.explanation: The learner must segment completed and remaining portions of one task.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Use part-whole completion contrasts to test tense without relying on isolated time-word matching.
simplificationConstraints: Keep the completed-part versus future-remainder contrast.
depthAdjustmentStrategies: Remove the explicit 'this afternoon' and establish past time through dialogue sequence.

evidenceReferences.quoteOrDescription: 'this afternoon' marks the completed work; 'I’ll finish it by Friday' reserves only the remainder for the future.

questions.skillExplanation: Q22 asks why Philip left the house; the passage states that Jason was hungry, Philip could not cook, and Philip therefore took him out for food.
reasoningOperations: Locate the causal chain before Philip leaves.
Resolve Jason as Philip's hungry little brother.
Map 'take Jason out for some food' to buying/getting food for him.
questions.questionMechanism: The answer is near-explicit but requires linking the brother's hunger and Philip's inability to cook to the departure.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: Distractors reuse later-story entities such as the woman, father, and police, rewarding chronology-aware reading rather than keyword matching.
questions.correctRationale: Philip went out because Jason was hungry and Philip could not cook, so he took Jason out for food; D is correct.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Jason was hungry; Philip couldn't cook; 'So Philip decided to take Jason out for some food.'

A.rationale: Philip did not know the woman and only encountered her after returning home.
A.misconceptionTarget: Pulling a salient later character backward into the cause.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The woman appears after the trip.

B.rationale: The father was known to be working late; Philip did not leave to search for him.
B.misconceptionTarget: Substituting a relevant person for the stated purpose.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The passage explicitly gives food as the purpose.

C.rationale: The police were already outside when Philip returned and were not the reason he left.
C.misconceptionTarget: Confusing later consequence with earlier motivation.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Police involvement occurs after Philip comes back.

studentFailureModes: Answering from the most dramatic later event.
Ignoring the causal connector 'So.'
misconceptionsTargeted: Story importance equals causal relevance.
Later events can explain earlier motivations without textual support.

shallowRecall.explanation: The answer is explicit but requires causal and referential integration across adjacent sentences.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Place the true motivation just before a later dramatic event so distractors can exploit salience without being ambiguous.
simplificationConstraints: Keep Jason's hunger and the explicit decision to get food.
depthAdjustmentStrategies: Remove 'So' and require readers to infer the causal link from hunger plus inability to cook.

evidenceReferences.quoteOrDescription: Jason was hungry; Philip couldn't cook; 'So Philip decided to take Jason out for some food.'

questions.skillExplanation: Q23 asks why Philip's father was angry; his quoted protest centers on the police treating him as a wrongdoer and refusing to believe that he was entering his own house.
reasoningOperations: Read the father's quoted protest as evidence of his grievance.
Connect the police's disbelief to his repeated insistence that he did nothing wrong.
Distinguish trigger from background facts such as forgotten keys.
questions.questionMechanism: The cause of emotion is inferred from dialogue and narration rather than stated in a single 'because' clause.
questions.whyTheQuestionWorks: Forgotten keys explain why he used a window, but the anger is directed at being disbelieved; this separates causal layers.
questions.correctRationale: The father shouts that he did nothing wrong, and the passage says the police did not believe him until Philip explained; their disbelief is the immediate reason for his anger, so C is correct.

correctEvidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: Father shouted 'I didn’t do anything wrong!' and 'the police didn’t believe him until Philip...explained everything.'

A.rationale: Forgetting the keys caused the unusual entry method, but his anger is expressed toward being treated as suspicious.
A.misconceptionTarget: Confusing an earlier enabling condition with the emotional trigger.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The quoted protest focuses on innocence and disbelief.

B.rationale: The woman stood behind the police because she was scared; she was not described as hiding from the father.
B.misconceptionTarget: Transforming a spatial detail into an unsupported intention.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: The passage says she stood behind the police.

D.rationale: Nothing in the father's speech shows anger that his sons went out; Philip's explanation actually resolves the police's suspicion.
D.misconceptionTarget: Attributing parental anger by stereotype instead of textual evidence.

evidenceRefs.quoteOrDescription: His shouted words concern entering his own house.

studentFailureModes: Choosing the earliest cause in the chain rather than the cause of anger.
Projecting common parent-child conflict onto the story.
misconceptionsTargeted: Any causal predecessor is an acceptable answer to an emotion question.
Dialogue can be ignored when narration provides background events.

shallowRecall.explanation: The learner identifies an emotion trigger by integrating dialogue with the police's behavior.

questions.reusableDesignPrinciple: Create layered causal chains where one fact causes an action and a later response causes the character's emotion.
simplificationConstraints: Preserve the father's protest and the police disbelief.
depthAdjustmentStrategies: Make the police disbelief implicit through their actions rather than stating it directly.

evidenceReferences.quoteOrDescription: Father shouted 'I didn’t do anything wrong!' and 'the police didn’t believe him until Philip...explained everything.'
